title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
hookLine: the prophetess leads the women in song and dance

lines: WHO PACKS A DRUM TO FLEE?
A WOMAN PICKS UP HER DRUM.
cards: Who packs a drum when they're fleeing slavery in the middle of the night? Unrisen dough, children, whatever can be carried, a few minutes' notice. And somebody, more than one somebody, brings a hand drum.
Then they cross the sea on dry ground. They stand on the far shore, shaking, looking back at the water.

And before anyone has worked out what to say, a woman picks up her drum, and the other women follow her out with their drums, dancing. Someone had planned for a celebration before there was anything to celebrate.

teach.h: MARY THE PROPHETESS, SISTER OF AARON.
teach.b: First, her name and her title. In the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin: "So Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand." Mary.
The same name: Miriam in Hebrew, Mariam in Greek, Maria in Latin. The mother of Jesus carries this woman's name. And the text calls her a prophetess.

teach.h: A TOF: A HAND DRUM FOR DANCING.
teach.b: In Hebrew it's a tof, a hand drum, a round frame with skin stretched over it, held in one hand and struck with the other. Not a harp in a temple. A traveling instrument, made for dancing in the open.

Third, the song. The chapter opens with a long song of Moses. Miriam's is short, two lines, and she sings it back to the women: sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.

teach.h: TWO LINES THAT ECHO MOSES'S SONG.
teach.b: It's the opening of Moses's song, almost word for word. What one voice began, she hands to everyone, with a drum to keep the beat. Fourth, where Catholics still sing it.

teach.h: STILL SUNG AT THE EASTER VIGIL.
teach.b: At the Easter Vigil, right after the crossing of the sea is read, the people answer with this song: let us sing to the Lord, for he has covered himself in glory.

And the Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours as a morning canticle. Miriam led the song on the far shore. Her namesake, Mary, would sing her own song of praise centuries later, about a God who lifts up the lowly.

how: At the Easter Vigil, after the reading of the crossing of the sea, Catholics sing the Song of Moses and Miriam from Exodus 15 as the responsorial psalm, and the same canticle is prayed in the Liturgy of the Hours.

games.q: you're Miriam on the far shore of the sea. the people are stunned and silent. Moses has just finished his song. what do you do?
o: wait for the men to finish celebrating.
take your drum and lead the women out in song and dance.
start packing for the journey ahead.
games.why: she takes the timbrel and all the women follow her with drums and dances, and she sings the refrain back to them.

practice: Choose a line you already know, a verse of a hymn, a refrain from Mass, the alleluia, a line of a psalm, or a line of thanks in your own words to any tune, and tap its rhythm on your knee like a drum.

Sing it once, out loud if you can, even quietly, then again a little stronger. If you pray, let it be praise for something you've come through; if you don't, let it be a song for anyone who made it to the far shore.

wordCard.voice: Miriam's timbrel. The hand drum of Miriam the prophetess, who led the women in song and dance on the far side of the sea. Today's word.
